chapter: First bands, Ennis, Thornhill and the Army
title: Joining Claude Thornhill's orchestra in 1942
summary: Gil describes Thornhill's large orchestra as a fine workshop and how Skinny Ennis's connections and a Maxine Sullivan arrangement led to the job.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: What was it like working for Thornhill?

It was a fine workshop for me. It was a full orchestra which is not easy to get to you know, to work to unless you are at school, for that. We had a french horn, two french horns, two trombones, two trumpets, five saxophones, three flutes, a tuba and a piano, drums, bass, guitar, bass. So it was a great opportunity for me to, uh...

Through Skinny Ennis this man who had the band in California, I met Claude Thornhill and I was sent to him to write for the orchestra. Skinny [Ennis] had one of those managers you know, who would sit back
and twirl his moustache and say, 'who is the greatest arranger in the World, the vocal arranger in the World?'
At that particular time California had a 'Loch Lomond,' hit record out with Maxine Sullivan, and we had made an arrangement for her.

So he said, okay, send for him. So he came out to California and that's how I met him. He worked there (Clawde (Skinny?)) on the Bob Hope Show one season and then he decided to go back to working with his own orchestra. So I was (pestering him and would write to him asking for a job?). So finally his arranger got drafted and he sent for me.
Although this was about a year before they got, or less than that, before everybody got drafted, about '42.
And then after the War came back again.
